name: Niger
card_headline: Niger's junta says it contained a 29 August mutiny; Russia's Africa Corps reportedly helped, while jihadist attacks reach the capital.
card_summary: General Abdourahamane Tiani, in power since the July 2023 coup, rules under a five-year transition with no election date and no political parties. Soldiers mutinied in Niamey on 29 August; the government says it regained control, and Russia's Africa Corps reportedly helped. Two jihadist groups attacked the capital's airport in 2026. ACLED counted 1,939 deaths in Niger in 2025. The IMF completed a positive programme review in July, and the US approved $414 million for a uranium mine in September.
card_local: Local sourcing is thin in this draft. AFP, citing a Téra resident and a former local elected official, reports at least 37 civilians killed near Téra on 12 November. Fratmat (Abidjan) and Seneweb (Dakar) supply regional reporting on the July ambush and the mutiny. [1][2][3]
card_international: AP and Reuters report the 29 August mutiny and the Russian role. Reuters reports that the US Development Finance Corp approved up to $414 million for the Dasa uranium mine. [4][5][6]
card_scholar: ACLED's Heni Nsaibia told AFP a significant fall in Tillabéri violence in 2026 is unlikely, and Critical Threats says ISSP and JNIM are likely outbidding each other with high-profile attacks. [7][8]
context_md: Soldiers led by General Abdourahamane Tiani overthrew elected President Mohamed Bazoum on 26 July 2023. [9] Niger left ECOWAS in January 2025, and in March 2025 Tiani was sworn in as transitional president for five years, with multiparty politics abolished by decree. [10] French soldiers were ordered out in 2023, and Washington agreed to withdraw about 1,000 troops two years ago; Reuters says the junta turned to Russia for security support. [6] Niger is the world's seventh-largest uranium producer, according to Reuters, and its oil leaves through a 1,950 km pipeline to Benin. [6][11] Jihadists first arrived in the western Tillabéri region in 2017, and that region now accounts for about two thirds of conflict deaths. [7]

sections.title: Jihadists have reached Niamey: about 1,300 of 1,939 deaths in 2025 were in Tillabéri
sections.body_md:
ACLED recorded 1,939 deaths in Niger in 2025, nearly 1,300 of them in Tillabéri region. About half came from clashes between jihadist groups and Nigerien forces, and half from attacks on civilians. [7] ACLED analyst Heni Nsaibia told AFP that a significant reduction in Tillabéri in 2026 is unlikely. [7] ACAPS, drawing on ACLED data, counts about 712 deaths in violence against civilians in 2025, against about 312 in 2023 and 333 in 2024, and says Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) drove most recorded fatalities in Tillabéri, ahead of state forces and JNIM. It also notes a reported airstrike on a market at Kourfeye on 22 September 2025 that killed about 40 civilians, with no public official findings at the time of writing. [12]

In 2026 the war moved onto military targets and the capital. ACLED's Ladd Serwat wrote that ISSP attacked Niamey's airport and airbase on 29 January, and that reports differ on whether attackers used mortars and RPGs or a drone; a drone would be ISSP's first in Niger. [13] Critical Threats says ISSP overran bases at Inates and Banibangou on 17 June, with sources reporting at least 51 and 34 soldiers killed, and that JNIM attacked Niamey's airport the next day, killing at least 11 soldiers and two civilians. Those authors warn that ISSP, JNIM and pro-government sources give very different casualty figures. [8] On 17 July an ambush on the Bankilaré to Téra road killed 16 soldiers by the Defence Ministry's count, while RFI, citing its own sources, reports at least 47. [2] On 12 November, AFP reports, armed men killed at least 37 civilians near Téra, and no group was named. [1]

The next front is the south. An ACLED study reported by Reuters found that violent incidents involving Islamist groups in the Niger, Benin and Nigeria border area rose 90 percent between 2024 and 2025, with deaths more than doubling to over 1,000. Niger's government did not respond to Reuters. [14]

lenses.local: Fratmat in Abidjan relays the Defence Ministry's and RFI's competing tolls for the July ambush and says they are hard to verify, and AFP's 12 November account rests on a Téra resident and a former local elected official. [2][1]
lenses.international: AFP and Reuters carry the November killings and the ACLED border-zone findings. [1][14]
lenses.scholar: ACLED, ACAPS and Critical Threats supply the counts, and Critical Threats says ISSP shifted toward security forces in 2026 and that both groups are expanding south. [12][8]

sections.title: A junta without a date for elections survived a mutiny with Russian help, and blames France
sections.body_md:
Gunfire and explosions began at Niamey's airport, which houses Base 101, around midnight on 28 to 29 August, and shots were also heard near the presidential palace, AP reports. The Defence Ministry said soldiers took comrades hostage and fired on sensitive sites, without giving a cause. [4] Defence Minister Salifou Mody later called it an outburst by a group of soldiers, according to RFI. [15] State television described hundreds of disaffected soldiers. Reuters, citing three sources, says Russia's Africa Corps played a key role in retaking the base, and one source said Russian forces used kamikaze drones. Russia's foreign ministry said Niger's army, with Africa Corps help, repelled the attack, and Algeria's defence ministry said it sent four fighter jets. [5] AP reports the Africa Corps has an estimated 200 to 300 personnel in Niger, mainly protecting the junta. [4]

No full toll has been published. AP reports that dozens of soldiers were arrested or killed, and RFI's correspondent reported state television showing nearly a hundred captured soldiers. [4][15] After a council of ministers on 4 September, RFI says the government acknowledged civilian deaths for the first time, thanked Mali, Burkina Faso, Algeria and Russia, and again accused France of backing the mutiny with local accomplices. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot dismissed the claim as pure fantasy. [16] Seneweb, relaying Jeune Afrique, reports that young officers commanding units from Tillabéri and Dosso were involved; that account is unconfirmed. [3]

Analysts point to the front line. Wassim Nasr of the Soufan Center told AP the mutiny was led mostly by soldiers deployed against jihadists, citing insecurity, mass killings of soldiers, food rations and poor equipment. [4] Rida Lyammouri of the Policy Center for the New South said there are no clear signs the military is bringing stability, and argued the junta has put protecting its power ahead of security. [17] There is no election to test any of this: HRW says the transition has been extended with no roadmap to elections. [9]

lenses.local: RFI and Seneweb are the regional reporters on the mutiny, and the Defence Minister's statement and footage of captured soldiers both came from Niger's state television. [15][3]
lenses.international: AP and Reuters agree that Africa Corps helped retake the base, and AP and Al Jazeera quote the Russian ambassador, Viktor Voropaev, on a request for help. [4][5][17]
lenses.scholar: ACLED's Heni Nsaibia says mass-casualty attacks on the army are becoming commonplace and will fuel unrest, and Control Risks' Beverly Ochieng says stability depends heavily on army cohesion. [17][4]

sections.title: Parties dissolved, critics stripped of nationality, and a media owner missing since 31 August
sections.body_md:
HRW says the junta dissolved all political parties and several independent unions in the past year, suspended dozens of civil society groups, and used a cybercrime law to detain journalists. [9] Bazoum, his wife and other figures remain detained. HRW reports that UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention opinions in February 2025 and May 2026 found the detentions of Bazoum and rights defender Moussa Tiangari arbitrary. [9] At its UN human rights review the government rejected recommendations to free people held arbitrarily, saying the Bazoum cases fall exclusively under national jurisdiction and denying that anyone is arbitrarily detained. [18]

On 17 September Tiani signed a decree provisionally stripping five exiled figures of Nigerien nationality, among them former Prime Minister Ouhoumoudou Mahamadou. HRW says the decree rests on a 2024 terrorism-database order and conflicts with the 1984 Nationality Code, and cites Niger's state press agency for a total of 25 people deprived under that order. [19] HRW also reports a 2026 penal code that sets 5 to 10 years in prison for consensual same-sex relations. [9]

The press has taken the sharpest hit. RSF ranks Niger 120th of 180 in 2026, down from 83rd. [20] On 8 May the media regulator ONC suspended nine France-based outlets, among them France 24, RFI and AFP, citing content likely to seriously undermine public order; CPJ says no legal article was cited. [21] Moussa Kaka, head of the Radio Télévision Saraounia group, was last seen leaving work in Niamey on 31 August, and CPJ says its requests for comment to the communication ministry and government spokesman went unanswered. [22] RSF reports that in early October the Justice Minister told the UN that Kaka is alive and held, which RSF calls arbitrary detention. [20] Kaka was arrested in October 2025 with five other journalists. [23]

lenses.local: Studio Kalangou, run by Fondation Hirondelle from a Niamey newsroom, is relayed by 52 private and community radio stations, but its output under the new regulator was not checked. [24]
lenses.international: CPJ and RSF are the main sources on Kaka, and the government gave CPJ no reported comment. [22][23]
lenses.scholar: HRW's World Report 2026 is the closest systematic source: it records the dissolution of parties and unions, the expulsion of the ICRC and detentions of journalists in 2025. [10]

sections.title: Uranium and oil: Niger is renegotiating who profits, with Orano, CNPC and now Washington
sections.body_md:
The junta treats resources as a sovereignty issue. The Somaïr mine at Arlit is 63.4 percent owned by Orano and 36.6 percent by state-owned SOPAMIN. Orano says an ICSID tribunal ruled on 23 September 2025 that Niger must not sell uranium produced by Somaïr, and that Niger's Council of Ministers had announced plans to nationalise the venture. Orano also says its representative has been held since May 2025. This is Orano's account, and Niger's response is not given in the article read. [25]

On 17 September 2026 the US Development Finance Corp approved up to $414 million in debt financing for the Dasa uranium project, owned by Canada's Global Atomic, according to the developer. Reuters sources say US Ambassador Kathleen FitzGibbon urged Washington to rebuild ties, and that Global Atomic has explored a northern export route through Algeria because of security risks. [6] The Rio Times reports a further deal lifting Niger's stake in the Madaouela project to 40 percent and a refinery concession near Dosso signed on 15 August; that summary is uncorroborated here. [26]

Oil is the other lever. Daba Finance reports that on 18 May Niger signed memoranda with Chinese partners to end a year of tension with CNPC: Niger takes 45 percent of the pipeline company WAPCO, the transport fee falls from $27 to $15 a barrel, an estimated $106 million a year in savings, and Nigeriens' share of management posts rises from 30 to 60 percent. Output has stabilised at about 110,000 barrels a day through the 1,950 km pipeline to Benin. [11] The IMF says higher oil revenue in 2026 is to be used to cut the deficit and meet social and food security needs. [27]

lenses.local: Daba Finance of Abidjan is the regional business outlet read on the CNPC deal, and no Nigerien outlet on it was located. [11]
lenses.international: Reuters, via Al Jazeera, carries the US financing, and World Nuclear News carries Orano's account of the tribunal ruling. [6][25]
lenses.scholar: SWP says the junta revoked Orano's licence in 2024 and nationalised Somaïr in 2025, and lists ECOWAS and UEMOA sanctions, the Benin border closure and aid cuts as economic pressure. [28]

sections.title: The IMF programme is on track and growth is high, with security named as the main risk
sections.body_md:
The IMF Executive Board completed the ninth review of Niger's Extended Credit Facility on 29 July 2026 and approved an immediate disbursement of about $33 million, bringing cumulative disbursements to about $342 million. The Fund calls programme performance generally strong, and says all periodic quantitative performance criteria were met at end-December 2025. [27] It estimates real GDP growth at 6.9 percent in 2025 and projects 6.7 percent in 2026. [27] It puts the fiscal deficit including grants at 3.3 percent of GDP in 2025 and 3.7 percent in 2026, and public and publicly guaranteed debt at 45.6 percent of GDP in 2025. [27] The authorities committed to clear all external arrears by end-2026. [27] The IMF lists heightened security threats as a downside risk. [27]

Conflict shows up in local prices and farm incomes. FEWS NET reports that millet in two Tillabéri markets averaged 290 CFA francs a kilo against a national average of 221, and that reduced cultivated areas in Tillabéri and Diffa have kept farm wages below average. It adds that a Middle East conflict may raise fuel and freight costs and so the price of imported rice, wheat and fertiliser. [29] The IMF page does not give security spending figures, and no Nigerien budget document was read for this draft.

lenses.international: The IMF is the main source and rates programme performance as generally strong while naming security as a risk. [27]
lenses.scholar: FEWS NET is the main technical source on how conflict affects markets, wages and prices in the west and southeast. [29]

sections.title: About 2.6 million people need aid while the NGO presence shrinks
sections.body_md:
The 2026 humanitarian plan counts about 2.6 million people in need across 32 of Niger's 63 departments and targets 1.6 million. It asks for $449 million, about 25 percent less than the 2025 budget. Its drivers are armed violence, floods and drought, epidemics such as cholera, access restrictions and funding cuts. The figures reflect late 2025. [30]

Displacement counts differ by source. ACAPS reports about 943,000 forcibly displaced people hosted at 31 December 2025: about 459,600 internally displaced people, about 436,000 refugees and asylum seekers and about 47,400 others of concern. [12] FEWS NET reports 1,032,135 displaced in February 2026, 53 percent internally displaced and 42 percent refugees. [29] FEWS NET puts Tillabéri, Diffa and north-west Tahoua in IPC Phase 3, crisis, mainly because of conflict, and says needs peak in the July to September lean season. [29] ACAPS reports about 2.22 million people, 8 percent of the population, in IPC Phase 3 or worse in the June to August 2025 lean season, and about 1.6 million children projected to suffer acute malnutrition between August 2025 and July 2026. [12]

The aid system is shrinking. ACAPS says the authorities ordered the ICRC to stop operations in early 2025, that about 135 organisations remained authorised in mid-November 2025 against more than 300 international NGOs before, and that on 7 January 2026 authorities announced the dissolution of several hundred more NGOs and associations. [12]

lenses.international: OCHA's plan and FEWS NET are the main sources on needs, and ACAPS documents the shrinking aid presence. [30][29][12]
lenses.scholar: ACAPS finds civilian harm concentrated in Bankilaré, Gothèye, Say, Téra and Torodi, with spillover into Dosso and Tahoua. [12]

sections.title: Algeria's jets, a thaw with Benin and an alliance of juntas shape Niger's room to move
sections.body_md:
Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso left ECOWAS in January 2025 and now form the Alliance of Sahel States. [10] After the mutiny the alliance issued a statement of full support, Algeria pledged solidarity and sent fighter jets and a transport aircraft, and Türkiye called for restraint. [4][17] It is unclear whether Mali or Burkina Faso gave direct military help. [17]

Benin and Niger formalised a commitment to reopen their shared border on 18 June, after talks in Niamey between Benin's President Romuald Wadagni and Tiani produced a nine-point plan. The border has been closed since the 2023 coup, and Niger had accused Benin of harbouring French bases. A committee will examine the conditions for reopening. [31] That thaw follows a claim Tiani made on state television after the January airport attack, when he accused France, Benin and Côte d'Ivoire of sponsoring it without offering evidence. [32] The fact-check section covers it.

Western ties are being rebuilt by deal rather than by troops. HRW says the US, Russia, Türkiye and Italy have prioritised security cooperation without rights benchmarks. [9] SWP says Germany halted most security cooperation after the coup, and argues that Europe should re-engage with the juntas pragmatically and drop democratisation as a short-term goal. It also cites a survey in which 64 percent of Nigeriens opposed the presence of foreign troops. [28]

lenses.international: Africanews reports the Benin communiqué, and AP and Al Jazeera report Algeria's and Türkiye's reactions to the mutiny. [31][4][17]
lenses.scholar: SWP and Crisis Group both treat the Sahel juntas as a bloc whose expansion and external ties Europe now has to deal with. [28][33]

Tiani is sworn in as transitional president for five years and multiparty politics is abolished by decree.
An ICSID tribunal orders Niger not to sell uranium produced by Somaïr, according to Orano.
Six journalists are arrested over a social media post about a solidarity fund for security forces.
ISSP attacks Niamey's airport and airbase; Tiani later blames France, Benin and Côte d'Ivoire.
The media regulator suspends nine France-based outlets.
Niger signs memoranda with Chinese partners that give it 45 percent of the oil pipeline company.
ISSP overruns military bases at Inates and Banibangou; JNIM attacks Niamey's airport the next day.
Benin and Niger formalise a commitment to reopen their border.
An ambush on the Bankilaré to Téra road kills 16 soldiers by the official count.

The US approves up to $414 million for the Dasa uranium mine; Tiani strips five exiles of nationality.
Armed men kill at least 37 civilians near Téra.

scores.coverage_basis: AP, Reuters and AFP file on Niger around major events such as the August mutiny, the airport attacks and the US uranium financing, with little steady flow in between [4][5][6]. ACLED, ACAPS and Critical Threats produce regular research [12][8], while Nigerien press access is restricted, with RSF ranking the country 120th of 180 [20].

severity.basis: ACLED counted 1,939 deaths in 2025, and in 2026 ISSP overran bases and JNIM and ISSP both struck Niamey's airport [7][8].
About 2.6 million people need aid and about 1 million are displaced or refugees, while the NGO presence has shrunk [30][29][12].
Parties are dissolved, there is no election roadmap, five more critics lost their nationality in September and Moussa Kaka has been missing since 31 August [9][19][22].
The IMF estimates 6.9 percent growth and public debt of 45.6 percent of GDP, with security as a downside risk, while conflict raises food prices locally [27][29].
A mutiny in the capital, a JNIM attack on Niamey's airport and ISSP's base assaults all fell within the last six months [4][8].

parts.basis: Russia's Africa Corps protects the junta, the US approved $414 million for a uranium mine, China's CNPC runs the oil pipeline and Orano is in arbitration [4][6][11][25].
Niger is the world's seventh-largest uranium producer according to Reuters, and its oil output is about 110,000 barrels a day [6][11].
ACLED finds Islamist violence in the Niger, Benin and Nigeria border area rose 90 percent between 2024 and 2025, and both groups are expanding south [14][8].
Niger hosts about 943,000 forcibly displaced people and sits on migration and insurgent corridors, though this draft found no source on outbound flows [12].
Niger left ECOWAS, is withdrawing from the ICC and has defied an ICSID order in a nationalisation dispute, according to HRW and Orano [10][18][25].

summary: Niger matters beyond its borders through uranium, a pipeline to the Atlantic coast, Russia's military foothold and an insurgency spreading toward Benin and Nigeria, more than through trade volumes [6][11][4][14].
gi.up: A fall of Niamey or a successful attack on the oil pipeline, or a large new outflow of refugees or migrants.
gi.down: A stabilised army, a reopened Benin border and a credible transition timetable.

gaps: Local sourcing is thin: no Nigerien outlet (Tamtaminfo, ActuNiger, Libération, Niger Inter, ONEP or Le Sahel) was opened; the local entries are regional outlets in Abidjan and Dakar and a Studio Kalangou project profile.
The mutiny toll, the number of arrests and Tiani's public reappearance after 30 August were not found; the Russian role rests on unnamed sources in Reuters and on Russian and Nigerien statements.

Displacement counts differ (about 943,000 forcibly displaced in ACAPS at end-2025, 1,032,135 in FEWS NET for February 2026) and the methods were not reconciled; humanitarian figures are from late 2025 and no 2026 IPC analysis was read.
The 17 July ambush toll differs (16 by the Defence Ministry, at least 47 by RFI sources) and the June base casualties are disputed; neither was independently confirmed.
The Madaouela stake and the Dosso refinery concession rest on one secondary summary (The Rio Times); the CNPC terms rest on one Abidjan business outlet, not on the memoranda.
HRW's July release says Niger left the ICC in June and its September page says Niger began withdrawing; the two were not reconciled and the timeline omits the ICC step.
Moussa Kaka's status after early October rests on RSF's report of a statement by the Justice Minister to the UN; the original statement was not found.
The Crisis Group JNIM report was read only as a catalogue entry, and the SWP study through a summary of its first 100,000 characters.
No Nigerien government primary documents (council communiqués, budget, charter) were read, and the 2026 budget and security spending are missing.
The January airport-attack article on Yahoo carries no date or agency, and the podcast episodes are from 2023 because no 2026 episode on Niger was verified.

reporters.name: Chinedu Asadu
reporters.bio: Bylined the AP's 30 August 2026 account of the Niamey mutiny, published on PBS NewsHour.
reporters.why: The report sets out the timeline, the Africa Corps role and analysts' views of the mutiny in one place.
reporters.label: AP via PBS NewsHour

reporters.name: Ilaria Allegrozzi
reporters.role: Senior Sahel researcher, Human Rights Watch
reporters.bio: Quoted in HRW's 23 July 2026 release on three years of military rule and in its 22 September release on nationality stripping.
reporters.why: HRW's Niger releases are the main documented record of detentions, press arrests and the nationality decrees.
reporters.label: Human Rights Watch

reporters.name: Heni Nsaibia
reporters.bio: Told AFP in March 2026 that ACLED expects no significant fall in Tillabéri violence in 2026, and was quoted by AP and Al Jazeera on the army's unrest after the mutiny.
reporters.why: Gives the most cited quantitative reading of the insurgency, from ACLED's event data.
reporters.label: Africanews (AFP)

reporters.name: Ladd Serwat
reporters.bio: Wrote ACLED's 2 February 2026 Expert Comment on the Niamey airport attack and the question of drone use.
reporters.why: Compares ISSP, ISWAP and JNIM drone use and weighs conflicting reports of the 29 January attack.
reporters.label: ACLED

reporters.name: Liam Karr and Alexandre Colas des Francs
reporters.bio: Authors of the 25 June 2026 Africa File on JNIM and ISSP attacks in Niger.
reporters.why: Sets out how the two groups compete and where ISSP is building support zones.
reporters.label: Critical Threats

reporters.name: Serge Daniel
reporters.bio: Credited as RFI's regional correspondent on the 30 August report of arrests after the mutiny and bylined the 5 September report on the council of ministers.
reporters.why: One of the few reporters whose accounts of the government's own statements reached French-language readers.
reporters.label: RFI via AllAfrica

reporters.name: Aboubakar Bamba
reporters.bio: Bylined the 22 July 2026 report on the Tillabéri ambush and the pressure on the junta.
reporters.why: Sets the Defence Ministry's toll beside RFI's higher figure for the July ambush.
reporters.label: Fratmat via AllAfrica

reporters.name: Moussa Kaka
reporters.role: Head of Radio Télévision Saraounia group, Niamey
reporters.bio: RSF says he founded Radio Saraounia in 1999 and a TV channel in 2011, and that he has been missing since 31 August 2026.
reporters.why: His case is the clearest current test of press freedom under the junta.
reporters.label: Reporters Without Borders

reporters.name: Rida Lyammouri
reporters.role: Analyst, Policy Center for the New South
reporters.bio: Quoted by Al Jazeera on 30 August 2026 on the junta's priorities after the mutiny.
reporters.why: Argues that armed groups are expanding toward the Benin and north-east Nigeria borders.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

books.title: Niger: Personal Rule and Survival in the Sahel
books.author: Robert B. Charlick
books.why: Routledge lists it as covering Niger's origins and history and has a chapter on the Nigerien political system. Older than the current junta; Routledge also lists a 2020 release.
books.label: Routledge

books.title: From Slavery to Aid: Politics, Labour, and Ecology in the Nigerien Sahel, 1800-2000
books.author: Benedetta Rossi
books.why: Follows the Ader region of Niger from slavery to aid dependence. The listing shows a December 2017 paperback.
books.label: MIT Press Bookstore

books.title: Historical Dictionary of Niger
books.author: Abdourahmane Idrissa and Samuel Decalo
books.why: A fourth-edition reference work with more than 700 entries on history, politics, economics and culture. Predates the 2023 coup.
books.label: Bookshop.org

podcasts.show: Deep Dish on Global Affairs (Chicago Council on Global Affairs)
podcasts.title: Sahel in Crisis: Niger's Coup and the Failure of Western Intervention
podcasts.guest: Kamissa Camara, US Institute of Peace
podcasts.why: Background on why the Sahel was vulnerable to coups and on Western security assistance. It predates the 2025 and 2026 events.

podcasts.title: Putsched out: Niger's coup d'etat
podcasts.why: A short episode on the coup and Niger's alignment with Russia, from the week it happened.

media.title: Sahel: Homeland or Death (Sahel: La Patrie ou La Mort)
media.creator: Pedro Stropasolas (Brasil de Fato)
media.where: Premiered in Sao Paulo; the link is a People's Dispatch article, and no streaming link was verified.
media.why: Interviews with 23 grassroots leaders from Burkina Faso, Niger, Mali and Benin. People's Dispatch presents it as a counter to French and mainstream narratives, so treat it as an advocacy source.

factchecks.claim: France, Benin and Côte d'Ivoire sponsored the January 2026 attack on Niamey's airport.
factchecks.by: Gen. Abdourahamane Tiani, in a state television address
factchecks.evidence: Yahoo's report says Tiani gave no evidence and records no reply from the three governments. ACLED says the Islamic State's Nashir newsletter credited ISSP with the 29 January attack, and Critical Threats also attributes it to ISSP.

sources.title: Niger leader blames France, Benin, Côte d'Ivoire for airport attack
Reported drone use in the Niamey airport attack would be a first for ISSP in Niger
Africa File (JNIM, al-Qaeda and ISSP in Niger)

factchecks.claim: France backed the 29 August mutiny in Niamey with local accomplices.
factchecks.by: Niger's government, at the 4 September council of ministers
factchecks.evidence: RFI reports the government made the accusation and that France's foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, dismissed it as pure fantasy. AP's first account links the mutiny to soldiers' grievances over deaths at the front, rations and equipment, and its text contains no claim about France. None of the reports read presents documentary evidence either way.

sources.title: Niger: Une semaine après la mutinerie... un conseil des ministres pour faire le point
Inside the 24-hour mutiny that threatened Niger's ruling junta and how Russian forces intervened

factchecks.claim: Niger can sell uranium produced by the nationalised Somaïr mine.
factchecks.by: Niger's government, which announced plans to nationalise the venture
factchecks.evidence: Orano says an ICSID tribunal ruled on 23 September 2025 that Niger must not sell uranium produced by Somaïr that was withheld in violation of Orano's rights. Orano is a party to the case, and the article read does not give Niger's response.

sources.title: Tribunal decision supports Orano in Somaïr dispute
Niger: au moins 37 civils tués par des "hommes armés" dans l'ouest

sources.note: Regional outlet; byline Aboubakar Bamba. Fraternité Matin is generally described as Ivorian state-owned; this was not verified in this session, so the flag is precautionary. Casualty figures are the Defence Ministry's and RFI's and are hard to verify.

sources.note: Covers events of 2025.

sources.title: Niger secures concessions from China's CNPC as oil output stabilizes
sources.note: Regional business outlet. Figures are the outlet's reading of the 18 May memoranda; the memoranda themselves were not seen.

sources.note: RFI is owned by France's public broadcaster. Byline Serge Daniel. The accusation against France is the Niger government's; the rebuttal is France's foreign minister.

sources.title: Niger's military-led government says it contained mutiny: What next?
sources.note: Al Jazeera is Qatar state-funded.

sources.note: The page read carries no byline and no attribution inside the text to HRW.

sources.title: Niger: Junta strips 5 more exiled critics of nationality
sources.note: News release datelined Nairobi; no individual author named. Ilaria Allegrozzi is quoted.

sources.title: Niger country page, World Press Freedom Index 2026

sources.title: Niger suspends 9 French media outlets for alleged public order threat

sources.title: Moussa Kaka, missing in Niger: four decades of journalism and campaigning for press freedom

sources.title: Studio Kalangou (Niger)
sources.note: The foundation is Swiss; the newsroom is in Niamey. This is a project profile, not a news report, and no Studio Kalangou bulletin was read.

sources.title: Tribunal decision supports Orano in Somaïr dispute
sources.note: Older than 12 months; used for the ICSID baseline. The account is Orano's, which is a party to the dispute. Niger's response is not given.

sources.title: Niger explained 2026
sources.note: Undated secondary summary; used only for items not found elsewhere (Madaouela stake, refinery concession). Not corroborated in this draft.

local_md:
Fratmat in Abidjan relays the Defence Ministry's and RFI's competing tolls for the July ambush and says they are hard to verify, and AFP's 12 November account rests on a Téra resident and a former local elected official. [2][1]

RFI and Seneweb are the regional reporters on the mutiny, and the Defence Minister's statement and footage of captured soldiers both came from Niger's state television. [15][3]

Studio Kalangou, run by Fondation Hirondelle from a Niamey newsroom, is relayed by 52 private and community radio stations, but its output under the new regulator was not checked. [24]

Daba Finance of Abidjan is the regional business outlet read on the CNPC deal, and no Nigerien outlet on it was located. [11]
international_md:
AFP and Reuters carry the November killings and the ACLED border-zone findings. [1][14]

AP and Reuters agree that Africa Corps helped retake the base, and AP and Al Jazeera quote the Russian ambassador, Viktor Voropaev, on a request for help. [4][5][17]

CPJ and RSF are the main sources on Kaka, and the government gave CPJ no reported comment. [22][23]

Reuters, via Al Jazeera, carries the US financing, and World Nuclear News carries Orano's account of the tribunal ruling. [6][25]

The IMF is the main source and rates programme performance as generally strong while naming security as a risk. [27]

OCHA's plan and FEWS NET are the main sources on needs, and ACAPS documents the shrinking aid presence. [30][29][12]

Africanews reports the Benin communiqué, and AP and Al Jazeera report Algeria's and Türkiye's reactions to the mutiny. [31][4][17]
scholar_md:
ACLED, ACAPS and Critical Threats supply the counts, and Critical Threats says ISSP shifted toward security forces in 2026 and that both groups are expanding south. [12][8]

ACLED's Heni Nsaibia says mass-casualty attacks on the army are becoming commonplace and will fuel unrest, and Control Risks' Beverly Ochieng says stability depends heavily on army cohesion. [17][4]

HRW's World Report 2026 is the closest systematic source: it records the dissolution of parties and unions, the expulsion of the ICRC and detentions of journalists in 2025. [10]

SWP says the junta revoked Orano's licence in 2024 and nationalised Somaïr in 2025, and lists ECOWAS and UEMOA sanctions, the Benin border closure and aid cuts as economic pressure. [28]

FEWS NET is the main technical source on how conflict affects markets, wages and prices in the west and southeast. [29]

ACAPS finds civilian harm concentrated in Bankilaré, Gothèye, Say, Téra and Torodi, with spillover into Dosso and Tahoua. [12]

SWP and Crisis Group both treat the Sahel juntas as a bloc whose expansion and external ties Europe now has to deal with. [28][33]
